Wind carries sand up the windward stoss slope. Transport includes saltation, surface creep and suspension of sufficiently fine material. The drawn grains are enlarged direction markers.
Yardangs are streamlined erosional remnants, commonly aligned with prevailing erosive winds. Abrasion and deflation act with weathering and rock structure. They are not heaps of deposited dune sand.
The crescent tips lie downwind of the central crest. The centre leeward slip face is 32° at true scale; twice-enlarged relief makes it look steeper. Actual repose angles vary.
These invented ridges taper along the wind direction. Their shapes do not determine a wind speed or erosion rate.
Barchan: deposited sand, a gentler windward slope and a steeper lee slip face. Migration translates the chosen shape downwind without assigning a rate.
Yardang: rock carved into streamlined ridges, aligned broadly with the erosive wind.

Selected beach profiles illustrate possible net sediment gain or loss. Real cross-shore transport depends on wave period, height, grain size, beach slope and water level; a wave label alone does not predict the outcome.

Oblique swash and roughly downslope backwash can move grains alongshore. Alongshore currents also transport sediment. The groyne intercepts the illustrated supply, but bypassing and changing wave directions occur in real systems.

A spit is attached to land at one end and extends into water as sediment accumulates. A hooked end can reflect changing waves and currents. Growth is selected geometry, not a predicted rate or complete sediment budget.
Inspect the cave from the seaward side, then compare arch, stack and stump. Openings are cut into a solid rock body; the cave retains a back wall.
Swash moves grains obliquely up the beach; backwash returns downslope. The zigzag is one transport pathway, not the full nearshore circulation.
A spit extends from the shore into a bay. Change Spit extent to compare the attached deposit; the water beyond remains open.
Groyne on: illustrated grains are intercepted updrift. This does not create new sediment.

Planetary albedo is the fraction of incoming sunlight reflected to space. It includes atmosphere, clouds and surface.
Outgoing longwave equals surface radiation transmitted through the layer plus upward radiation emitted by the layer. At equilibrium it balances absorbed sunlight.

Several adjacent cirques can erode back towards a mountain summit, leaving a pyramidal peak. This prescribed three-basin form illustrates the relationship, not a surveyed mountain or a calculated erosion history.
A narrow ridge separates adjacent glacially eroded hollows or valleys. The ridge is a remnant between basins, not a deposited wall.

A bowl-shaped hollow with steep headwalls and a gentler floor can be eroded at the head of a glacier. The thin ice overlay and moving symbols only indicate a possible flow direction; thickness and rate are not solved.
Snow persisting across years compacts to firn and ice. The illustrated head is a source area, not a calculated equilibrium-line altitude.
Abrasion and quarrying by debris-bearing ice can broaden and deepen a valley. Hiding present ice exposes the selected bed; it does not simulate the rate or history of valley erosion.
This ridge marks a chosen earlier ice margin. Unsorted debris can accumulate at a margin that remains in roughly one position. A retreating glacier still moves its surviving ice down-valley.

A low-permeability layer confines the aquifer below 12 m. The blue pressure surface above it is the level in a well, not an extra water-filled layer.
The potentiometric surface is the level to which water rises in a well. The confined aquifer remains saturated beneath its lid.
The water table separates saturated pores below from an unsaturated zone above. The coloured surface is a level, not a hollow lake.
The pumping rate is imposed on a fully penetrating ideal well. In this steady experiment a fixed-head boundary supplies the withdrawal; it does not model long-term storage depletion.

Unconfined: blue marks the top of saturated pores.

Young end of the Yellowstone volcanic track. Its older volcanic centres extend southwest along the Snake River Plain. The three large caldera-forming eruptions at Yellowstone are not the entire hotspot history.
The southeastern end includes active Hawaiian volcanism. Kauaʻi, to the northwest, preserves rocks about 5–5.5 million years old. Not every volcano at a given island is the same age.
The southwest end of the recognised Yellowstone track reaches roughly 17 Ma. These five illustrated depressions are symbols, not surveyed caldera outlines or an eruption sequence.

Kauaʻi provides an approximately 5.5 Ma reference at the northwestern end of the main island comparison. The full Hawaiian–Emperor chain is much longer and older. These volcanic shapes are not island coastlines.

A plume hypothesis involves an upwelling thermal anomaly in mostly solid mantle. Partial melting can occur during ascent; this is not a hollow pipe or a column of liquid magma. Geometry and thermal colour are schematic.

A selected open passage lies within soluble rock. Dissolution can enlarge fractures and bedding-plane openings. Most of the landscape remains rock; it is not a hollow underground lake. Cave networks can be much more complex.
Clints are limestone blocks; grykes are enlarged fissures between them. Joint opening is exaggerated for inspection and changes a chosen geometry, not a calculated dissolution rate.

This surface depression is a solutional sinkhole example. Other sinkholes involve subsidence or collapse. Water can enter connected fractures and underground drainage; not all depressions open directly into a large cave.
Groundwater emerges where the connected drainage intersects the land surface. The route is schematic; it does not calculate hydraulic head, transit time or contaminant transport.
Cutaway exposes a selected passage and enlarged flow tracers.
The front rock face hides the passage; enable Cutaway to inspect it.
High relief and steep, rugged slopes characterise this mountain example. There is no universal height threshold separating all mountains and hills.
This hill has lower relief and gentler slopes than the mountain selected here. Height alone does not define every landform.
A plateau is an extensive relatively level high surface. Its edge may be steep, and rivers may dissect it; plateaux have different origins.
A plain has relatively low local relief. Plains can occur at high or low elevation; this selected example is low.
A basin is a depression relative to its surroundings. It can have an outlet or internal drainage; the shape alone does not guarantee a lake.

Permafrost is ground remaining at or below 0 °C for at least two consecutive years; it is not necessarily pure ice. This section assumes established permafrost below the active layer.

Winter thermal contraction opens cracks. Water entering them can refreeze and add ice veins over repeated years. This differs from simply expanding all water by 9%, and from a glacier eroding a valley.

This seven-cell pattern with uneven margins shows the topology of an ice-wedge network. Natural polygons are irregular. Lines locate wedge margins below the surface; they are not a layer of exposed blue ice covering the ground.

Headward erosion extends this lower valley towards a divide. When the divide is breached, a new lower route can divert the neighbouring river. Relative base level, rock and structure affect the process.
A reduced local stream may occupy the former valley. An elbow of capture and an underfit valley are clues; neither proves capture without other geomorphic and geological evidence.
Before capture: two separate drainage routes.
Headward erosion: the captor approaches the divide.
After capture: headwater flow turns into the lower outlet; the former downstream reach loses that supply.

This inner-bank deposit is on the inside of a bend. Secondary circulation, boundary shear and sediment supply shape erosion and deposition; a single surface-speed arrow cannot explain the entire cross-section.
Repeated overbank flows can deposit relatively coarse sediment near the channel, building low banks. These are sedimentary landforms, not constructed flood defences.
Fine material can travel farther in overbank flow. Natural levees and floodplain sediments vary with flow, sediment size, vegetation and repeated floods.
A delta can grow where sediment supply and deposition exceed removal and available space is filled. Channels split and shift; this three-branch pattern is an illustration.
Not every river mouth builds a delta. Tides, waves, sea-level history and sediment supply can maintain an estuary. Neither receiving water nor the absence of tides alone determines the outcome.
Separate enlarged vessel: the global timeline spans 20 minutes. The grain position uses the stated Stokes settling speed through 2 m of still fresh water. The vessel is not at the landscape scale.
Inner-bank point bar within a curved channel. Flow tracers move downstream; the selected bar is not growing.
A sediment-built delta with branching distributaries meets standing water. This is one mouth type; estuaries are different receiving environments.

Turbulent flow can circulate sediment against bedrock and excavate a hollow. Stones shown here are enlarged tracers; some potholes also grow through suspended sediment abrasion and hydraulic processes.

Igneous rock forms by cooling and crystallisation of melt. This coarse-grained texture is illustrative, not a scan or a mineral identification.
This clastic sedimentary example is bedded. Compaction and cementation can lithify sediment; chemical and biological sedimentary rocks have other pathways.
This foliated example illustrates solid-state recrystallisation and deformation. Not all metamorphic rocks are foliated, and melting is a separate process.
Loose sediment is material that can be transported and deposited. Grain sizes are enlarged. It is not yet a lithified sedimentary rock.
Magma is melt that may contain crystals and gas. It becomes igneous rock on cooling and solidification, not merely by becoming hotter.

Basalt forms at the spreading centre and moves away with each flank. Decompression generates partial melt below; it does not turn the whole mantle into a magma ocean.
Age increases with distance from the axis: age = distance / half spreading rate. This ideal experiment has equal rates on both flanks.
A stripe of the same age is found at the same distance on the opposite flank. Its width depends on both reversal duration and spreading rate.

The eye has relatively light winds, subsidence and often reduced cloud. It is surrounded by the strong winds and deep convection of the eyewall; it is not a funnel touching the sea.

Calcite reacts with carbon dioxide and water to give dissolved calcium and bicarbonate. Symbol particles do not show actual ion size, concentration or stoichiometric counts.

A fixed water mass occupies about 9% more volume as ice. The joint walls are allowed to move in this geometric experiment; real cracking depends on confinement, water supply, stresses and rock strength. Ice segregation is another important frost-weathering mechanism.

These are idealised stages of ocean-basin opening and closure. A basin need not complete every stage or close along the same boundary; this is not a prediction of the Atlantic’s future.
The unstretched reference continent is about 35 km thick in this section. Rifted margins are simplified; continental collision thickens the crustal root.
Lithosphere includes crust and rigid upper mantle. The section separates crust composition from mantle; it does not represent the mantle as a magma ocean.
Extension and spreading can open a basin.
Oceanic lithosphere subducts; continental crust is not simply swallowed in the same way.
Collision thickens and deforms the continental crust; remnants of an ocean may remain in the suture.
